faqs.q: There is a dead animal smell in my Lexington walls. What should I do?

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Lexington?

faqs.q: There is a snake in my West Columbia yard. Can you tell what it is?
faqs.a: Start with identification, not panic. Around West Columbia, the everyday snakes are non-venomous rat snakes and racers; the caution species are the copperhead, which is statewide and the venomous snake we encounter most in the Upstate and Midlands. Keep distance, bring pets in, and tell us the size, pattern, and where it sheltered. We identify from photos or on site, handle non-listed snakes where appropriate, and treat venomous encounters as safety work. Reducing cover and rodent food near the foundation lowers repeat sightings more than any single capture.

faqs.q: An opossum keeps getting under my West Columbia house. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: Opossums den under houses because crawlspaces near Saluda and Congaree riverfront neighborhoods across from downtown Columbia are dry, dark, and close to pet food and trash. One opossum is mostly a nuisance; a season of them brings droppings, torn insulation, and fleas. We trap the animal — opossums are handled under depredation rules, since routine relocation is not permitted in South Carolina — then screen vents and repair the crawlspace door so the shelter is gone, not just the tenant.

Structure decides the labor, since older housing near Saluda and Congaree riverfront neighborhoods across from downtown Columbia often hides several entries behind additions and repairs. Season decides the timing, especially when litters or bat pups mean part of the work waits a few weeks. You get the full picture from the inspection before committing to the plan.

West Columbia.wildlife_intro:
West Columbia keeps our crew busy around the Saluda and Congaree riverfront neighborhoods across from downtown Columbia. Two problems account for most visits: bats behind shutters and in gable vents, and skunks denning under decks.

Postwar brick and frame homes, lake and river cottages, and newer subdivisions share the same streets, with pine canopy hanging over most roofs. Hot summers and mild winters keep Midlands wildlife moving most of the year, and the spring litter season turns small roof gaps into denning calls within weeks.

Removal without repair does not hold in West Columbia, so our visits pair the animal work with sealing and screening sized to the house itself.

faqs.q: We found an opossum in our Cayce crawlspace. What happens next?
faqs.a: In Cayce, opossums move into crawlspaces through broken vents and loose doors, then rotate dens every few days, which is why sightings come and go. We trap at the access point, remove the animal under SCDNR depredation rules, and seal the full foundation line. Securing pet food and trash at night removes the other half of the attraction.

faqs.q: We have rats in our Cayce attic. How is that different from squirrels?
faqs.a: Rats work at night and squirrels work at dawn, which is the first clue. In Cayce, roof rats climb from trees, vines, and utility lines around Congaree River and creek neighborhoods south of the Gervais Street bridge, while Norway rats burrow along foundations and come up through plumbing gaps. We identify the species, trap inside the structure, and seal the entry points at roof and foundation level — poison alone leaves dead rats in walls and does nothing about the openings.

faqs.q: How do you price the work on a Cayce home?
faqs.a: Honestly, it depends on what the inspection turns up — and in Cayce that is rarely just one hole. Attic contamination, the number of openings to seal in steel, crawlspace repairs, and whether the job needs return visits for trapping all shape the work. We itemize what we find, explain which items stop the problem for good and which are optional, and let you decide with the full list in hand.

Older homes near the town center give way to ranch subdivisions and then to farmhouses on the outskirts, and the wildlife entries change with each ring. Pine straw is the Midlands detail that matters most: copperheads vanish into it, armadillos root through it, and raccoons cross it nightly from creek woods to rooftops.

Before we leave a Cayce home, the roofline, foundation line, and any outbuilding we worked on get rechecked opening by opening — that recheck is what keeps one call from becoming three.

faqs.q: Why do squirrels keep getting into Irmo attics?
faqs.a: Gray squirrels need an opening little more than an inch wide, and the usual doors here are soffit corners, gable vents, and the gaps where additions meet the main roof, reached from fences and overhanging limbs. Trapping without sealing just invites the next squirrel, so our crew fits one-way doors, lets the animals leave, and seals every opening in steel — timed so a nursing litter is never sealed inside.

faqs.q: I found a raccoon in my Irmo attic — can you move it to the woods?
faqs.a: We do not promise that, because South Carolina does not allow it: SCDNR states that routine relocation of wildlife is against state law, and a captured animal must be destroyed or, with a separate department permit, may be relocated. What our crew does is eviction and exclusion — the raccoon leaves through a one-way door or is removed under SCDNR depredation rules, and then we seal every entry in steel so the attic stays closed. Raccoons are also South Carolina's leading rabies carrier in the Department of Public Health's testing, so attic latrines get cleaned and sanitized, not just emptied.

faqs.q: When can bats be removed from a Batesburg-Leesville home?

What controls the timing is SCDNR guidance, which we follow: complete exclusions are planned for early spring (March-April) or fall (August-October), and we do not run a full exclusion from May through mid-July, sometimes into August, because flightless pups would be trapped inside. That window is agency guidance, not a state law. We can inspect and map every entry at any time of year, and a bat found inside your living space is different — keep the room closed and call us, because bats in living quarters are a rabies-testing situation handled with the Department of Public Health.
